metadata.title: Overfitting, When a Perfect Score Lies
metadata.audience: makers and curious learners new to ML

beats.narration_text: Namaste, this is Liam, in for Bear. The ask: my model scored zero error on its training data. Perfect. Should I trust it? Show me with real numbers.

show.event: composer card fades in on cream
greeting 'Namaste, Liam' types above the composer
the ask types in
runningText 'fitting sixteen noisy points…' appears
three result lines cascade in; '9,882.6' is the one terracotta moment

props.segment: Overfitting, When a Perfect Score Lies
props.command: My model scored zero error on its training data. Perfect. Should I trust it? Show me with real numbers.
output: the honest grade comes from data the model never saw

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — ask lands answered; Liam introduced in first breath.

beats.narration_text: A perfect training score can mean memorized noise. A model flexible enough to pass through every point it was shown has learned the points, not the pattern, and stumbles on the next one.

show.event: cream page holds; caret blinks
types 'A perfect training score / means a perfect model.'
'means a perfect model' turns terracotta, hesitates, backspaces
types 'can mean memorized noise'
final lines settle: 'A perfect training score / can mean memorized noise.'

props.text:
A perfect training score
means a perfect model.

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW — misconception corrected: a perfect score on the data you trained on is not evidence of a good model; it can be evidence of memorized noise.

beats.narration_text: Here's the setup. A smooth curve, the truth, which the model never gets to see. Sixteen points drawn from it, each knocked off by random noise: that's the training set. A thousand more, drawn the same way and locked away: the test set. The model fits the sixteen. We grade it on the thousand it has never seen.

show.event: axes draw on, x from −1 to 1
dashed curve y = sin(πx) draws on; tag 'the truth (hidden from the model)'
16 ink dots drop onto the curve, then each jumps off it by its noise; faint tick joins each dot to the curve
bracket chip: 'training set · 16 points'
60 faint hollow dots (preview of the 1,000) fade in beside, then slide into a box labelled 'test set · 1,000 points · locked'
the dashed truth curve fades to 40% (the model can't see it); labels 'fit on these' under the training dots and 'grade on these' under the test box; 'grade' is terracotta

shot.visual_intent: The data-generating picture: hidden true curve, 16 noisy training points, a locked 1,000-point test set.
shot.motion_claim: Each dot visibly leaves the curve by its own noise, so 'noise' is a seen displacement, not a word.

beats.narration_text: The grade is one number, the mean squared error. For each point, take the gap between the real value and the model's guess, and square it, so misses above and below both count, and big misses count most. Then average over every point. On the training points, that's training error. On the test points, test error. Zero means every point was hit exactly.

show.event: MathTex typesets: MSE = (1/n) Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ (yᵢ − f̂(xᵢ))²
box spotlight on yᵢ: 'real value'; box spotlight on f̂(xᵢ): 'model's guess'
box spotlight on the '−' and the square: 'gap, squared'
worked term slides in under the equation: one training point, the line's worst miss: gap -1.032, squared 1.065
box spotlight on (1/n) Σ: 'average over all 16': 4.546 ÷ 16 = 0.284
two chips under the equation: 'on training points → training error' | 'on test points → test error'
chip 'MSE = 0 · every point hit exactly'; the spotlight box moves onto it

shot.visual_intent: The error measure, typeset, with a glossary spotlight per symbol and one real worked term.
shot.motion_claim: Box spotlights walk the formula in narration order; the worked term is a real point from the data.

beats.narration_text: Fit three models to the same sixteen points. A straight line, degree one, is too stiff: it misses the bend, at about zero point two eight in training, zero point two seven on test. Degree three follows the curve: zero point zero six, and zero point zero four seven. Degree fifteen has sixteen coefficients for sixteen points, so it threads every one. Training error: zero. Test error: almost ten thousand.

show.event: three panels side by side, the same 16 dots in each; headers 'degree 1', 'degree 3', 'degree 15'
left: straight line draws through the dots; counters train 0.284 | test 0.273
middle: cubic draws, hugging the hidden curve; counters 0.059 | 0.047
right: degree-15 curve threads every dot, swinging off the panel between them (clipped at the frame, arrow marks the exit)
right counter train → 0
right counter test spins up to 9,882.6 in terracotta

shot.visual_intent: Underfit, good fit, overfit on identical data, with executed train/test errors under each panel.
shot.motion_claim: The three curves draw in narration order; the degree-15 curve visibly passes through every dot and leaves the frame between them.

beats.narration_text: Do that for every degree from zero to fifteen. Training error, in ink, only ever goes down: a more flexible model can always fit the same points at least as well. Test error falls too, at first. It bottoms out around degree three to six, just above the dashed line, which is the noise itself. Then it turns, climbs, and leaves the chart. That U is overfitting.

show.event: axes: x 'degree 0–15', y 'error 0–0.6'; dashed floor line at 0.040: 'noise floor: even the true curve scores 0.04'
ink training-error dots land degree by degree, stepping down to 0 at 15
test-error dots land degree by degree, falling with the ink ones
minimum ringed at degree 5: 0.0466
test dots climb, then exit the top from degree 11; terracotta exit chips 1.8 · 26.4 · 5,807.1 · 8,251.1 · 9,882.6
label 'overfitting' and chip 'same shape in 500 fresh datasets' land in the empty upper right

shot.visual_intent: Training vs test error across all 16 degrees, executed on the film's dataset, with the noise floor.
shot.motion_claim: The two series land degree by degree so the divergence happens on screen; the test curve leaves the chart.

beats.narration_text: Here's where the simple story bends. Is degree fifteen just too complex? Keep the model, and add data. At twenty points, test error drops to about twenty-nine. At a hundred, zero point zero four eight. At a thousand, zero point zero four one, right on the noise floor, and training error has risen from zero to meet it. Complexity alone isn't the problem. Complexity the data can't pin down is.

show.event: the degree-15 panel from B04, wild curve over 16 dots; counter n = 16
dots multiply to 20; curve refits; test counter 28.8
dots multiply to 100; curve calms; test 0.048
1,000 dots; curve lies on the hidden truth; test 0.041
both counters meet at the dashed 0.040 floor; terracotta ring on the meeting point

shot.visual_intent: One fixed degree-15 model tamed by more data (nested training sets, executed).
shot.motion_claim: The same model refits live as the data grows; train and test errors converge on the floor.

beats.narration_text: One more way a score can lie. Say you try all sixteen degrees and keep whichever scores best on a held-out validation set. Now that score helped choose the model. Across a thousand repeats, it came in better than the real error seven times in ten. The fix: choose on validation, then report on a test set nobody touched. That lands about half and half, as an honest score should.

show.event: data strip splits into three labelled blocks: 'train 30 · validation 20 · test 20'
sixteen degree chips 0–15 appear; validation's pick (the most-picked degree) gets a box
left panel 'choose and report on validation': a 10×10 grid of 100 trials fills; optimistic trials fill terracotta
left counter: 70% optimistic; median reported 0.0439 vs real 0.0508
right panel 'choose on validation, report on untouched test' fills the same way
right counter: 55% optimistic; median 0.0506 vs 0.0508; reference chip 'degree fixed in advance: 53%'

shot.visual_intent: Selection bias from reusing a held-out score, measured over 1,000 executed repeats, with a control.
shot.motion_claim: The two trial grids fill side by side and are held together, so the 70 vs 55 comparison is seen.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Training error grades the model on answers it has already seen. Test error, on data held back, is the honest grade. As flexibility grows, training error falls; test error falls, then climbs. A perfect training score can mean the noise was memorized. More data lets a flexible model behave. And a score you chose by is spent, so keep one test set untouched.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Using only Python and NumPy, draw sixteen points from y equals sine of pi x on the interval from minus one to one, with Gaussian noise of standard deviation zero point two, plus a thousand more as a test set. Fit polynomials of degree zero to fifteen and print the training and test error for each. Repeat with two hundred training points. Then, from the printed numbers only, tell me which degree you would ship in each case, and how you chose it. Here's what to check. Training error should never go up as the degree rises. With sixteen points, degree fifteen should score essentially zero in training and something enormous on test. And watch how Claude picks the degree. If it picks by the test error, ask it what it should have used instead.

props.command: Using only Python and NumPy, draw 16 points from y = sin(pi x) on the interval from -1 to 1, with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.2, plus 1000 more as a test set. Fit polynomials of degree 0 to 15 and print the training and test error for each. Repeat with 200 training points. Then, from the printed numbers only, tell me which degree you would ship in each case, and how you chose it.
output: check: training error never rises as the degree goes up
check: 16 points, degree 15 → training error ≈ 0, test error huge
check: the degree is chosen without peeking at the test set
